opus-5.5.text:
From what I saw, the core of it is that he wants to get as close to the actual engineering as possible. He doesn't want a polished slide deck from a manager who's two or three layers removed from the work. He wants to talk to the person who designed the part, wrote the code, or ran the test, because that person knows where the real problems are.

So the meetings tend to be very direct and very technical. He'll ask why something is designed a certain way, and if the answer is "that's the requirement," he'll push on who set that requirement and whether it actually makes sense. That's his first-principles habit: question every requirement, delete parts or steps that don't need to exist, and only then optimize what's left. A lot of engineers, me included at first, instinctively jump to optimizing something that maybe shouldn't be there at all.

There's also a strong sense of urgency. The question is always "what's the limiting factor, and what would it take to get it done much faster?" It can feel intense, but I think the intent is to force clarity. If you can't explain the bottleneck simply, you probably don't understand it well enough yet.

My takeaway was less about him as a person and more about the mindset. Stay close to the ground truth, be honest about what's not working, and don't hide behind process. For something as hard as a humanoid robot, where hardware, software, and AI are all tangled together, that kind of directness really helps the team move.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to understand is that Elon doesn't treat meetings as a reporting layer. At Optimus, when he sits down with engineers, it's not "give me the slide deck and the status." He wants the person who actually touched the actuator, the tendon design, the control loop, in the room, and he goes straight to the physics of the problem.

So the pattern looks roughly like this. He'll pick one component and ask, why does this cost what it costs, why does it weigh what it weighs, why is this requirement even here? And if the answer is "that's what the spec said" or "that's how the previous version did it," that's basically a failure. He pushes until you either defend the requirement from first principles or you admit it can be deleted. A lot of the design changes on Optimus, like consolidating actuator types or simplifying the hand, came out of exactly those conversations where someone was asked to justify a part and couldn't.

The second thing is speed. He hates the gap between decision and action. If a question gets resolved in the meeting, the expectation is that the change starts that afternoon, not after a planning cycle. That's uncomfortable if you come from a traditional robotics lab where you'd write a proposal first.

The third thing, which people underestimate, is that he's genuinely technical in these rooms. He'll argue about motor torque density or gearbox efficiency with the person who designed it. Engineers either find that energizing or terrifying, and that self-selects the team pretty hard.

Now, is it a good approach? I'd say it's extremely effective for a hardware program that needs to move from prototype to mass production fast, because it kills bureaucracy and forces clarity. The downside is that it can be brutal on people, and sometimes the "delete this part" instinct overshoots and you have to add it back later. Elon himself says that if you never add anything back, you're not deleting enough. So the churn is partly by design.

If I had to summarize it in one line: he runs engineering meetings like a debugging session on the product and the organization at the same time, and the engineer in front of him is expected to know the truth down to the first principles.

astra-6.text:
The way I understand it, he wants the meeting to get directly to the engineering problem. What’s blocking progress? Is it a physical limitation, a design choice, or a requirement that doesn’t actually need to exist? Then, what can we test to find out?

For something like Optimus, that means being ready to explain why you made a decision, rather than just reporting that a task is on schedule. I’d characterize the approach as questioning assumptions and pushing toward concrete evidence. But I can’t speak firsthand to how those meetings actually run.
